I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

vignette:
Aroha's Assault and the Unraveling

Aroha Te Kanawa was forty-two years old when a man with a knife cornered him in the stairwell of a commercial building in downtown Portland. It was 4:47 p.m. on a Tuesday in March-a time he would come to dread with the kind of animal certainty that bypassed thought entirely. He had stayed late to finish rewiring the third floor of an office complex, a job he'd taken pride in. The building was quiet. Most people had left. When he heard the footsteps behind him on the landing, he had turned, and in the space of what felt like seconds-though he would later struggle to know if it was thirty seconds or three minutes-the man had forced him against the concrete wall, pressed the blade against his ribs, and taken his wallet and watch. Aroha had given them without resistance. What he couldn't stop replaying, what burned in his mind in disconnected flashes, was the man's face very close to his own, the smell of cigarettes and something else he couldn't name, the weight of the blade, the sound of his own breathing, which seemed impossibly loud. Then the man was gone, running down the stairs, and Aroha was alone, intact but fundamentally altered in ways he wouldn't fully recognize for weeks.

The first month after the assault, Aroha had tried to work through it. His partner, Marcus, had encouraged him to see someone, but Aroha had resisted, telling himself that it was just an unlucky thing that had happened, that he needed to move past it. Instead, he began to notice that 4:47 p.m. arrived each day like a weight descending. His chest would tighten. His mouth would go dry. He would find himself reaching for his phone-scrolling through Reddit, playing games, watching videos that meant nothing to him-anything to push the time through without thinking. By five o'clock, the worst of it would pass, and he would feel a kind of exhausted relief.

By the sixth week, Aroha's phone screen time had become a kind of second job. He would sit on the couch beside Marcus, thumb moving mechanically, his mind nowhere and everywhere at once. Marcus had asked, gently at first and then with frustration, what was wrong. Aroha didn't have an answer that made sense. He also didn't tell Marcus that he had started drinking most evenings-a beer, then two, sometimes a whiskey-to soften the edges of 4:47 p.m. and to help him sleep, though the sleep that came was thin and fractured.

The avoidance had spread like a slow infection. Aroha stopped taking new jobs in unfamiliar buildings. He told his boss he preferred residential work, which paid less and offered less variety. When Marcus suggested they try a new restaurant in a neighborhood Aroha didn't know, he invented an excuse. He couldn't map the exits in his mind. He couldn't assess where the danger was. The thought of being in a space where he didn't know the layout, where someone could come around a corner, where doors could open suddenly-it was intolerable. He began to avoid watching the news, and when Marcus would turn on a crime drama, Aroha would leave the room or pick up his phone, his jaw tight.

What unsettled him more than the avoidance itself was what he believed about why it had happened. Aroha had come to a quiet, settled certainty that the assault had occurred because of the kind of man he was. He had been alone in an unfamiliar building. He had stayed late. He had not been alert enough. Someone else-someone smarter, more careful, more aware-would have seen the danger coming. Would have left earlier. Would have taken a different route. This belief lived in him like a second assault, a constant low hum of self-recrimination that made him feel both culpable and helpless.

The fragmented memory haunted him most. When he tried to reconstruct what had happened, he saw only isolated images: the man's mouth moving, though he couldn't recall the words; his own hand against the wall; the flash of the blade. Whole sections were missing, as though his mind had simply declined to record them. He felt intense guilt when these fragments surfaced-guilt he couldn't fully articulate, as though he had done something wrong, as though he should have fought harder or been braver or simply been different.

By his eighth month post-assault, Aroha's startle response had become a source of shame. When Marcus touched him unexpectedly-a hand on his shoulder while he was at the sink, a brush against his back in bed-Aroha would flinch violently, his body bracing as if for attack. Marcus had stopped reaching for him. At work, when a colleague moved suddenly nearby, Aroha would jolt, his heart racing, his mind flooded with the sensation of imminent danger even in the bright safety of a residential kitchen. He had begun to feel that he had no future, that this fractured, hypervigilant version of himself was permanent, that the assault had simply revealed the truth of who he was-a man who was not equipped for the world, who had always been vulnerable, who would always be at risk.

It was Marcus, finally, who insisted. He had found Aroha at 4:45 p.m. one evening, phone in hand, already bracing himself, and something in Marcus's face-a mixture of grief and determination-had broken through. Aroha had agreed to seek help, though he carried with him the conviction that talking about it would change nothing, that he was fundamentally damaged, and that the best he could hope for was to learn to live in the smaller, safer version of his life that the assault had forced him into.
